teile.einleitung: Headphones are small loudspeakers that you wear directly on or in your ears. This lets you listen to music, films or games on your own without disturbing others. They come with or without a cable, big over the ears or tiny in the ear.
wichtigste: With headphones you hear sounds on your own without others having to listen too.
Listening too loudly can damage your ears permanently.
Headphones with a built-in microphone are called a headset.
Very small headphones that you put straight into your ear are called earphones.
Many wireless headphones connect via Bluetooth.
The letters L and R stand for the left and the right side.
In traffic you should not wear loud headphones, because then you cannot hear cars and bikes.

abschnitte.text: Each side of a pair of headphones contains a tiny **loudspeaker**, also called a driver. It turns electrical signals into sound by making a thin membrane vibrate back and forth. Because the loudspeaker sits so close to the ear, very little energy is enough for a good sound. The sides are marked **L** for left and **R** for right. That way you can hear in music and games which direction a sound is coming from.

**Over-ear** headphones are big and enclose the whole ear. On-ear models only rest on the ear and are a little lighter. **Earphones** are very small and are put straight into the ear, some with soft silicone tips. A **headset** also has a microphone so that you can make phone calls, play online or take part in video calls. There are also bone-conduction headphones, which carry the sound through the bones of the skull to the inner ear.

You plug wired headphones into the **headphone socket** on the computer, which usually has a diameter of 3.5 millimetres. Some devices use a USB connection instead. Wireless headphones usually connect via **Bluetooth**, a radio technology for short distances. They have a battery that you need to charge regularly. Many modern models also have active **noise cancelling**, which makes noise such as engine sounds on the train or plane almost disappear.

If you listen to music very loudly for a long time, you can damage your **hearing** permanently. In the inner ear there are fine hair cells that break when there is too much noise and do not grow back. A warning sign is a whistling or rushing sound in the ear, called **tinnitus**. A simple rule of thumb is: at most about 60 percent of the volume and a break after an hour. Many mobile phones now warn you themselves if you are listening too loudly.

In **traffic** you must be able to hear cars, bikes, trams and warning signals clearly. With loud headphones or strong noise cancelling you often notice them too late. So it is better to take your headphones off when cycling and crossing the road. Some headphones have a **transparency mode** that lets surrounding sounds through. But it does not completely replace paying attention.

As early as around 1910, the American Nathaniel Baldwin built headphones that were used by the navy. For a long time, it was mainly radio operators, telephone operators and pilots who used headphones. From 1979 Sony's portable cassette player, the **Walkman**, made light headphones popular with many people. Later came MP3 players and smartphones with earphones. Today wireless earphones are a completely everyday accessory.

teile.einleitung: Online advertising is advertising on the internet, for example on websites, in apps, in games or before videos. Companies pay to have their products shown to as many people as possible. If you can recognise online advertising, you are less likely to fall for tricks.
wichtigste: Many free apps and websites earn their money from advertising.
You can often recognise advertising by the word “Ad” or “Advert”.
A short advertising film, for example before a video, is called a commercial.
An influencer who is paid for praising something is also advertising.
You should not click on a flashing window saying “You've won!”.
The safest way to close an advert window is with the small X.
Not everything an advert promises is really true.

abschnitte.text: **Online advertising** is any kind of advertising you see on the internet. This includes pictures at the edge of a website, called **banners**, and windows that suddenly open, called **pop-ups**. Short advertising films before videos and paid posts on social networks also count. Even in search engines, paid results are often right at the top.

abschnitte.titel: Why is there so much of it?
abschnitte.text: Many apps, games and websites are free, but making them still costs money. That is why they show **advertising**, because companies pay for every advert or every click. This is how video platforms and search engines, for example, earn a lot of money. That is why people say: if something is free, you often pay with your attention.

Websites use small files, the **cookies**, to remember what you look at. From this they build up a picture of what you are interested in. Then you get **personalised advertising**, that is, adverts that match your own interests exactly. If you search a lot for football boots, you will often see adverts for football boots afterwards.

Some advertising is not honest or is even dangerous. Messages like “You've won! Click here!” are almost always a trick to steal data or sell something. There are also fake close buttons that actually open a new page. The safest way to close a window is with the small **X**, or you ask an adult.

Reputable websites label advertising with words like **Ad**, “Advert” or “Sponsored”. In games, advertising often appears as a video that you have to watch to get a reward. Programs that hide advertising are called ad blockers. It is important to stay calm, not to buy anything hastily and not to enter any personal details.

One of the first advertising banners appeared on an American website in 1994. Back then, many people still clicked on it out of curiosity. Today online advertising is one of the biggest advertising markets in the world. Large internet companies such as Google and Meta earn most of their money from **advertising**.
